edges.why: The statement says 'more' refers to the number in each group, and the learner finds those numbers by counting each group.
Matching objects one to one shows which group has leftover objects, so 'more' is judged by number and not by size or spread.
The statement contrasts a complete triangle or square with a gapped figure, so the learner must already see the intended shape.
Picking the named shape from a set of circle, square, triangle and rectangle requires telling the different shapes apart first.

numeral.digit-formation.root_reason: Copying digit forms from a card is a motor skill that needs no earlier number or shape skill in the map, only the ability to look at a form and reproduce it.

counting.number-words.vocabulary.root_reason: Telling number words apart from other words is vocabulary and needs no earlier counting or quantity skill, since the statement says reciting in order is not required.

edges.why: The test starts from two rows matched one to one and judged the same number, then asks whether spreading changes that sameness.
Knowing a count stays the same however the objects are arranged supports judging that spreading out leaves how many unchanged.
The test counts 8 socks and then counts 4 pairs, each time counting a collection to find how many, with the pair treated as one object.
The statement requires parts of equal length, and equal length is judged by laying lengths side by side as the test does.
The requirement that parts together fill the strip with no gaps or overlaps is the whole being all of its equal shares.
Comparing a/b with 1 uses the fact that 1 can be written as b/b, a fraction with the same denominator.
With 1 written as b/b, comparing a/b with b/b is a same-denominator comparison decided by the numerators.
The statement compares the numerator a with the denominator b as whole numbers to decide greater than, equal to, or less than.
Reading a/b as a copies of 1/b, and knowing that b copies of 1/b make 1, gives the comparison with 1.
The statement compares the number of unit fractions a with the number b that make 1 to decide the size relative to 1.
The statement reads the fraction bar between two fractions as division, extending a divided by b equals a/b.
A numerator and denominator that are themselves fractions only make sense if a fraction is a number that can be divided.
The statement defines the quotient through a = b x c, so the quotient is read as the unknown factor c.
Recalling a quotient without computing uses the known multiplication fact b x c = a for factors from 1 to 10.
The statement writes a decrease with a negative number, so the learner must already know a negative number as the opposite of a positive amount.
